title: Strengthening Forensic Science in the United States: A Path Forward
authors: Committee on Identifying the Needs of the Forensic Science Community (co-chairs Harry T. Edwards, Constantine Gatsonis)
key_findings: Concluded that many forensic disciplines need systematic scientific change: research on validity, enforceable standards, consistent best practice.
Recommended an independent federal entity (proposed National Institute of Forensic Science) to set and enforce standards, plus mandatory accreditation and certification.
Framed weak forensic practice as a contributor to wrongful convictions and a resource/governance problem, not only an individual-competence problem.
athar_applications: Anchor reference for every ATHAR 'limits of evidence' lesson and for the Validity Matrix.
Supports a design rule: each forensic method in a case must carry an explicit reliability tier.
limitations: US-focused; describes the state of the field in 2007-2008; the proposed NIFS was never created.
Does not rank disciplines numerically; later reviews (PCAST 2016, NIST foundation reviews) are more method-specific.

title: Forensic Science in Criminal Courts: Ensuring Scientific Validity of Feature-Comparison Methods
authors: President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST)
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Defined 'foundational validity' (empirically shown repeatable, reproducible, accurate with measured error rates) vs 'validity as applied'.

Found single-source and simple-mixture DNA foundationally valid; latent prints valid but with false-positive rates that could be as high as about 1 in 306 (FBI study) and 1 in 18 (another lab's study) as upper bounds.

Found bitemark analysis far from foundational validity; firearms short of it (one appropriate black-box study only, FP about 1 in 66, upper bound 1 in 46); footwear identifying-characteristic associations and hair comparison not established.
Complex-mixture DNA: subjective interpretation not valid; probabilistic genotyping valid only within limited conditions (3 contributors, minor contributor >=20%).
athar_applications: Primary basis for the Validity Matrix tiers and for teaching 'not all forensic methods are equally reliable'.
Gives concrete, age-appropriate numbers for upper-bound error rates usable in a fictional 'expert testimony' mini-game.
limitations: Strongly contested by DOJ, FBI and some practitioner bodies (see ATH-SRC-0303); its black-box-only validation criterion is debated.
Snapshot of 2016; later studies (e.g., ATH-SRC-0335 firearms) report new data; does not cover non-comparison disciplines (toxicology, pathology).

title: An Addendum to the PCAST Report on Forensic Science in Criminal Courts
authors: President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST)
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Approved 6 January 2017; restates that subjective methods need empirical (black-box) testing; experience or uniqueness claims cannot substitute.
Reports a further literature check (400+ papers, INTERPOL summaries) that did not change its conclusions on bitemarks, footwear, hair.
Notes closed-set firearms study designs greatly underestimate error rates; proposes a cross-cutting study group and NIST role.
athar_applications: Shows learners how science responds to criticism: a model for a 'peer review' mechanic in ATHAR.
limitations: Same contested framework as the main report; written by the same body defending its conclusions.

title: United States Department of Justice Statement on the PCAST Report: Forensic Science in Criminal Courts
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Argues pattern comparison is not metrology and categorical examiner conclusions are not measurements.
Rejects PCAST's requirement of multiple black-box studies with fixed criteria; favours convergent validity from the whole literature.
Argues a single error rate does not generalise across labs/examiners/cases; black-box studies lack casework quality controls such as verification.
athar_applications: Lets ATHAR present a genuine expert disagreement (PCAST vs DOJ) as a critical-thinking exercise for 16+ learners.
limitations: Position statement of a prosecuting agency, not peer reviewed; Innocence Project and Union of Concerned Scientists publicly requested its retraction (letters seen in search results, Feb/June 2021).
Document date not printed on the fetched text; 13 January 2021 date taken from the filename of the Innocence Project response letter (search result).

title: DNA Mixture Interpretation: A NIST Scientific Foundation Review (NIST IR 8351)
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Reliability of mixture interpretation is a matter of degree that depends on sample complexity (number of contributors, template amount, allele sharing).
Likelihood ratios are assigned, not measured; different analysts/software can give different LRs for the same profile.
A DNA association does not show how or when DNA was deposited (transfer); LRs should state propositions and assumptions; contamination control matters more as sensitivity rises.
Public validation and proficiency data are insufficient; proficiency tests mostly use simple samples.
athar_applications: Core source for the 'DNA is strong but not magic' module and the DNA transfer virtual lab.
Supports a game rule: complex mixtures yield graded, uncertain outputs, never a binary 'match'.
limitations: US-centred; technical; draft (2021) and final (Dec 2024) versions differ - use final.
Does not give a single numeric reliability threshold by design.

title: Bitemark Analysis: A NIST Scientific Foundation Review (NIST IR 8352)
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: None of three key premises is supported: uniqueness of anterior dentition at individual level; accurate transfer of patterns to skin; reliable analysis of features.
Examiners often disagree even on whether an injury is a bitemark; in one cited study of 39 analysts only 8% of cases reached 90% agreement on three key questions.
Concludes bitemark analysis cannot accurately exclude or not-exclude individuals as the source.
athar_applications: Flagship 'discredited method' example for teens; contrast with single-source DNA to show the spectrum of reliability.
limitations: Narrow scope (bitemark comparison only), not forensic odontology as a whole (dental identification of remains is a different, better-supported task).
Draft July 2022, final March 2023; odontology bodies published responses (NIST companion document summarises criticisms and responses - not separately verified).

title: Digital Investigation Techniques: A NIST Scientific Foundation Review (NIST IR 8354)
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Digital investigation techniques rest on established computer-science methods and are reliable when used appropriately.
Limitations: not all evidence may be found; deleted-file recovery may return extraneous material; OS/app updates change the meaning of artefacts over time.
athar_applications: Basis for ATHAR digital-evidence puzzles: timestamps, metadata and logs as interpretable but context-dependent clues (fictional data only).
limitations: Innocence Project and others commented on the draft (public comments document exists); review focuses on technique reliability, less on examiner interpretation/bias.

title: Latent Print Examination and Human Factors: Improving the Practice through a Systems Approach (NISTIR 7842)
authors: Expert Working Group on Human Factors in Latent Print Analysis
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology / National Institute of Justice
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Treats bias as unconscious and systemic, requiring procedural safeguards (blinding, blind verification) rather than exhortation.
Separates procedural error from outcome error; error measurement belongs in a quality system.
Advises against testimony that an identification excludes every other person in the world.
athar_applications: Template for an ATHAR 'lab management' mechanic: the player designs information flow to protect an examiner from context.
limitations: 2012 snapshot; written within a US system; recommendations not binding.

title: Forensic Handwriting Examination and Human Factors: Improving the Practice Through a Systems Approach (NISTIR 8282r1)
authors: Expert Working Group for Human Factors in Handwriting Examination
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Recommends contextual information management and blinding to task-irrelevant information.
Notes strict LSU may be harder in handwriting because relevant features are not always defined in advance.
Reports no consensus on how to express probabilities; discusses opinion scales vs likelihood-based scales and the need to disclose possibility of error.
athar_applications: Basis for a safe 'questioned document' lab with fictional handwriting and graded conclusion scales.
limitations: Revision 1 (May 2021) of the 2020 report; Working Group consensus document, not empirical study.

title: OSAC Registry (Organization of Scientific Area Committees for Forensic Science)
authors: NIST Organization of Scientific Area Committees for Forensic Science
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: At fetch (27 Oct 2026) listed 264 standards: 189 SDO-published and 75 OSAC Proposed; latest addition dated 06 Oct 2026.
Placement needs a two-thirds vote of the proposing subcommittee and the Forensic Science Standards Board after technical/quality review.
Owners include Academy Standards Board (98), ASTM (69), OSAC (75), SWGDE (12), ISO/IEC; 23 subcommittees (e.g., Human Forensic Biology 28, Trace Materials 34, Forensic Toxicology 16).
athar_applications: Use as the living reference for which standards exist per discipline; ATHAR content reviewers should cite registry status and version.
limitations: Counts change monthly; listing describes the US system; inclusion means OSAC endorsement, not proof of a method's validity.
Registry page is public; the standards themselves are owned/copyrighted by SDOs.

title: OSAC Forensic Science Standards Library
authors: NIST Organization of Scientific Area Committees for Forensic Science
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: At fetch the Library view listed 777 documents (264 on Registry, 45 archived, 394 SDO-published, 287 in SDO development; categories overlap).
The Registry is a vetted subset of the Library.
athar_applications: Lets reviewers distinguish 'on Registry' vs 'merely published' vs 'in development' when ATHAR cites a standard.
limitations: Counts are a moving snapshot; US-centred.

title: ANSI/ASB Standard 040: Standard for Forensic DNA Interpretation and Comparison Protocols
authors: Academy Standards Board (AAFS); text from OSAC Biology Scientific Area Committee
key_findings: Requires labs to have written DNA interpretation and comparison protocols that account for technical variables and the range of results expected from their sample types.
Status: published, First Edition 2019 (AAFS page); a revision document also appears on the AAFS site (search result) - current revision status to be checked on the OSAC Registry.
athar_applications: Teaches the principle that interpretation rules are fixed in advance (pre-registration of decision rules) - a design pattern for fair ATHAR lab tasks.
limitations: Download gated by a name/email form; price/licence not stated on page.
Protocol-level standard, not an empirical validity study.

title: ANSI/ASB Best Practice Recommendation 007-24: Postmortem Impression Submission Strategy for Comprehensive Searches of Essential AFIS Databases
key_findings: 2nd edition (2024), superseding 007-18; listed in OSAC Standards Library under Medicolegal Death Investigation as an SDO-published standard.
Addresses submitting postmortem fingerprints to all essential databases so that identification of the deceased is not missed.
athar_applications: Illustrates that much of forensic medicine is about identifying the dead and documenting, not 'solving' - useful framing for the forensic-medicine card (no imagery).
limitations: Operational practice document; low direct teen relevance; Registry status not explicit on fetched page.

title: ISO/IEC 17025:2017 General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories
key_findings: Edition 3, published 2017-11-29; reviewed and confirmed in 2023 (stage 90.93).
Sets requirements for competence, impartiality and consistent operation of labs; used by accreditation bodies as assessment criteria.
athar_applications: Explains to learners what 'accredited lab' means and does not mean (competence system, not a guarantee every result is correct).
limitations: Generic lab standard, not forensic-specific; does not by itself establish validity of a forensic method (see DOJ vs PCAST debate on validation).

title: ISO 21043-4:2025 Forensic sciences - Part 4: Interpretation
key_findings: Edition 1, published June 2025; applies to all forensic disciplines, to human-judgement and statistical-model opinions, at scene, lab or court.
Requires interpretation to address alternative propositions framed by the customer's questions; not needed when analysis directly answers the question (e.g., substance identified).
athar_applications: International anchor for ATHAR's 'two competing explanations' interpretation mechanic.
limitations: Paywalled; 14 pp.; adoption varies by country; content summarised from ISO abstract only.

title: ISO 21043-2:2018 Forensic sciences - Part 2: Recognition, recording, collecting, transport and storage of items
key_findings: Edition 1 (Aug 2018); at fetch ISO listed it at stage 90.92 'to be revised', expected to be replaced by ISO/DIS 21043-2.
Covers recognising, recording, collecting, transporting and storing items of potential forensic value, at scenes and in facilities; excludes digital data recovery (ISO/IEC 27037).
athar_applications: Principle-level basis for ATHAR's documentation/chain-of-custody mechanic (record before you touch; every handover logged).
limitations: Under revision - re-check before citing in product; paywalled.

title: A guide to ISO 21043 forensic sciences from the perspective of the forensic-data-science paradigm
key_findings: Describes ISO 21043's five parts: vocabulary; recovery, transport and storage; analysis; interpretation; reporting.
Reads the standard through the forensic-data-science paradigm: transparent, reproducible, bias-resistant methods, LR framework, empirical calibration and validation under casework conditions.
athar_applications: Shows ATHAR the direction of travel internationally: from 'expert says match' to calibrated, transparent reasoning.
limitations: Authors are advocates of one paradigm (forensic data science); not a neutral summary of all views.

title: ENFSI Guideline for Evaluative Reporting in Forensic Science
authors: European Network of Forensic Science Institutes (ENFSI)
key_findings: Approved version 3.0 (8 March 2015), produced by the EU-funded STEOFRAE project.
Four requirements: balance, logic, robustness, transparency; report probability of findings given propositions, not of propositions given findings.
Uses the likelihood ratio and a hierarchy of propositions (sub-source, source, activity, offence) with an indicative verbal scale from 'weak' (LR 2-10) to 'extremely strong' (LR >= 1,000,000).
Separates evaluative, investigative and technical reporting.
athar_applications: Core of ATHAR's evidence-weighing engine: every clue updates support between two competing explanations; verbal-scale UI.
limitations: Official PDF re-verified on enfsi.eu on 2026-10-27 (gap-fill): 128 pp., 'Approved version 3.0', dated 8 March 2015; listed under 'Evaluative Reporting' on enfsi.eu/documents/forensic-guidelines/ (upload date 2016-09-27). No later version was listed on that page.
Verbal scales are known to be misunderstood by lay audiences (see ATH-SRC-0318); LR framework is not universally adopted (e.g., in US practice).

title: Discussion on how to implement a verbal scale in a forensic laboratory: Benefits, pitfalls and suggestions to avoid misunderstandings
key_findings: Discusses benefits and pitfalls of verbal equivalents for likelihood ratios and how to avoid misunderstandings when implementing them in a lab.
athar_applications: Warns ATHAR UI designers: verbal labels ('strong support') can be read as probability of guilt - design explicit 'what this does NOT mean' tooltips.
limitations: Bibliographic record verified via Crossref; detailed findings summarised from title/known scope only - expert check needed.

title: Forensic science activities: statutory code of practice - version 2
key_findings: Version 2 published 5 June 2025, in force 2 October 2025 (388-page PDF); made under the Forensic Science Regulator Act 2021.
Version 1 published 13 March 2023, in force 2 October 2023, withdrawn 6 March 2026.
Sets quality standard requirements for forensic science activities related to criminal investigation and justice in England and Wales.
athar_applications: Shows teens that forensic quality is regulated by law in some countries - comparative civic-literacy content.
limitations: Jurisdiction-specific (England and Wales); very long operational document - use only at principle level.
GOV.UK content is usually under the Open Government Licence v3.0, but the licence for this PDF was not confirmed in-session.

title: Forensic Science Regulator Act 2021 (c. 14)
key_findings: Statutory basis requiring the Regulator to publish a code of practice for forensic science activities in England and Wales (per GOV.UK page, ATH-SRC-0319).
athar_applications: Context only: example of statutory forensic regulation for comparative modules.
limitations: Confirmed via search result and GOV.UK reference, not read in full.
AUDIT 2026-10-27: legislation.gov.uk states its content is available under the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated; rights corrected from UNKNOWN (attribution required).

title: Royal Society / Royal Society of Edinburgh courtroom science primers: Forensic DNA analysis; Forensic gait analysis
authors: UK judiciary (leads incl. Niamh Nic Daeid, Sue Black)
key_findings: Launched 22 Nov 2017: plain-English primers on forensic DNA analysis and forensic gait analysis, written by scientists and judges, peer reviewed by practitioners, including limitations.
Further primers (statistics, vehicle-collision physics) were announced as planned.
athar_applications: Model for ATHAR's tone: plain-language, limitation-first explanations co-written by scientists and lawyers.
limitations: Only the launch page was read; later primers (e.g., statistics, firearms, bitemarks) not verified in-session.
Written for UK judges, not teens.

title: The forensic confirmation bias: Problems, perspectives, and proposed solutions
publisher: Elsevier (Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition)
key_findings: Reviews how prior beliefs, expectations and context can bias collection, perception and interpretation of forensic evidence.
Proposes procedural remedies such as limiting examiners' exposure to irrelevant context and blind/sequential procedures.
athar_applications: Primary source for the 'bias in the lab' learning arc; justifies ATHAR's context-reveal mechanics.
limitations: Narrative review; effect sizes in casework remain hard to estimate.

title: Contextual information renders experts vulnerable to making erroneous identifications
key_findings: Experimental study in which experienced fingerprint examiners, unknowingly re-shown prints they had previously judged, changed conclusions when given misleading context (widely cited classic).
athar_applications: Basis for a safe lab: same fictional fingerprint pair shown with different 'case stories' to reveal context effects.
limitations: Very small sample of examiners; details of design (sample size) not re-checked in-session - expert should confirm numbers before use.

title: Cognitive and Human Factors in Expert Decision Making: Six Fallacies and the Eight Sources of Bias
key_findings: Six fallacies: bias is an ethical issue; only 'bad apples' are biased; expert immunity; technological protection; blind spot; illusion of control (awareness alone fixes bias).

Eight sources of bias in three groups: the case (data, reference materials, contextual information); the person (base rates, organisational factors, education/training, personal factors); human cognitive architecture.
athar_applications: Directly usable as a teen-friendly 'six myths about bias' module and as reflection prompts after each case.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical paper; taxonomy is influential but not itself an empirical test.
Citation confirmed via PubMed (PMID 32508089); listed there as free article.

title: Linear Sequential Unmasking-Expanded (LSU-E): A general approach for improving decision making as well as minimizing noise and bias
key_findings: Extends Linear Sequential Unmasking beyond comparative disciplines: examine raw evidence first, then reveal reference/context information in an order based on relevance, objectivity and biasing power, documenting each step.
athar_applications: Core design pattern for ATHAR: staged information reveal with commitment points (learner records an initial judgement before seeing more context).
limitations: Procedural proposal; limited empirical testing of LSU-E effectiveness in casework.

title: Context Management Toolbox: A Linear Sequential Unmasking (LSU) Approach for Minimizing Cognitive Bias in Forensic Decision Making
key_findings: Letter proposing LSU: analyse and document the questioned (crime-scene) evidence before seeing the reference sample, with controlled, documented unmasking.
athar_applications: Same as LSU-E: supports a 'commit before comparing' rule in ATHAR comparison labs.
limitations: Short letter, not an empirical study; title captured from Crossref may be truncated.

title: Cognitive bias and blindness: A global survey of forensic science examiners
publisher: Elsevier (Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition)
key_findings: International survey of forensic examiners' beliefs about bias; known for documenting a 'bias blind spot' (bias acknowledged in others more than in oneself).
athar_applications: Supports a reflective ATHAR prompt: 'Could I be biased here?' after confident conclusions.
limitations: Self-report survey; detailed percentages not re-checked in-session.

title: Subjectivity and bias in forensic DNA mixture interpretation
key_findings: Showed that DNA analysts given the same complex mixture without case context reached divergent conclusions, illustrating subjectivity in mixture interpretation (widely cited).
athar_applications: Key corrective to 'DNA is always objective': complex mixtures involve judgement.
limitations: Small number of analysts; predates widespread probabilistic genotyping; details not re-checked in-session.

title: Cognitive bias in forensic pathology decisions
key_findings: Two parts: a 10-year review of Nevada death certificates for children under six, in which 'homicide' rather than 'accident' was more often ruled for Black than for White children; and an experiment in which 133 forensic pathologists given identical medical information but different irrelevant context (child's race, caregiver) made biased manner-of-death decisions.
Published in J Forensic Sci 66(5):1751-1757 (2021); PubMed lists 23 published comment letters in the following issue.
athar_applications: Shows that bias concerns apply even to medical forensic judgements; ATHAR should avoid presenting 'the pathologist's verdict' as context-free.
limitations: Highly controversial: PubMed links 23 published comment letters (J Forensic Sci 66(6), 2021), many critical; the letters themselves were not read - treat conclusions as contested.
Sensitive subject (child deaths, race) - unsuitable as teen content; use only as an adult-reviewer reference.

title: Cognitive bias in forensic anthropology: Visual assessment of skeletal remains is susceptible to confirmation bias
key_findings: Experimental evidence that contextual information can shift visual assessments of skeletal remains (e.g., sex/age estimates).
athar_applications: Supports a safe virtual-osteology lab (stylised 3D bones, no real remains) with context-manipulation reveal.
limitations: Small participant pool including non-experts; details not re-checked in-session.

title: Accuracy and reliability of forensic latent fingerprint decisions
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
key_findings: 169 examiners each compared about 100 latent-exemplar pairs (pool of 744): false-positive rate 0.1% (5 examiners made FP errors); false-negative rate 7.5%, with 85% of examiners making at least one FN.
Independent re-examination caught all false positives and most false negatives; examiners often disagreed on whether prints were suitable for comparison.
athar_applications: Gives a real, balanced picture for teens: fingerprints are strong but not infallible; verification matters; 'inconclusive' is a legitimate outcome.
limitations: Volunteer examiners who knew they were tested; prints selected to be challenging but not casework-matched; PCAST used upper-bound estimates from this 'FBI study'.

title: Repeatability and Reproducibility of Decisions by Latent Fingerprint Examiners
key_findings: Follow-up to the 2011 black-box study measuring whether examiners repeat their own decisions over time and agree with each other (repeatability vs reproducibility).
athar_applications: Teaches the difference between 'same person, same answer later' and 'different experts, same answer' - two separate reliability questions.
limitations: Same participant pool constraints as ATH-SRC-0331; specific percentages not re-checked in-session.

title: Accuracy and reliability of forensic handwriting comparisons
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
key_findings: 86 examiners, 7,196 conclusions on a five-level scale: erroneous 'written by' on 3.1% of non-mated pairs; erroneous 'not written by' on 1.1% of mated pairs.
Errors on twins' writing much higher (8.7%) than non-twins (2.5%); less-trained examiners were more often definitive and made more errors.
athar_applications: Excellent basis for a fictional handwriting lab showing graded conclusions and the 'twins' hard-case effect.
limitations: Volunteer participants; US examiners; the definition of error depends on how 'inconclusive' and 'probably' categories are treated.

title: Accuracy of comparison decisions by forensic firearms examiners
key_findings: 173 examiners, 8,640 comparisons: estimated false-positive rates about 0.66% (bullets) and 0.93% (cartridge cases); false negatives about 2.87% and 1.87%.
Most errors came from a small number of examiners; beta-binomial model used due to examiner variability.
athar_applications: Shows ATHAR how post-PCAST research added data; frames firearms evidence as 'improving but debated' (no weapon handling content).
limitations: Critics (e.g., ATH-SRC-0335) argue reported error rates depend heavily on how inconclusive decisions are counted; a correction was published (DOI 10.1111/1556-4029.15580, 2024).
Online 2022, issue Jan 2023.

title: Inconclusives, errors, and error rates in forensic firearms analysis: Three statistical perspectives
key_findings: Examines how the treatment of 'inconclusive' decisions changes computed error rates in firearms black-box studies, comparing three statistical perspectives.
athar_applications: Advanced (18+) module: the same data can yield very different 'error rates' depending on definitions.
limitations: Abstract not captured in-session; summary based on title/scope - expert to confirm specific conclusions.

title: Wrongful convictions and claims of false or misleading forensic evidence
key_findings: Analysed 732 National Registry of Exonerations cases with false/misleading forensic evidence (1,391 examinations) and built an error typology.

Most errors were not examiner identification/classification mistakes; more often reports or testimony miscommunicated results, departed from standards or omitted limitations; non-lab actors (presumptive tests without confirmation, suppression by investigators) also contributed.
Estimated that better technology or testimony/practice standards might have prevented roughly half of these wrongful convictions.
athar_applications: Key finding for ATHAR: teach communication of limits, not just lab technique; build 'testimony review' tasks.
limitations: Based on exoneration cases (a non-random, US-only sample); author is NIJ-affiliated.

title: The Coming Paradigm Shift in Forensic Identification Science
publisher: American Association for the Advancement of Science (Science)
key_findings: Influential argument that traditional identification sciences relied on untested assumptions of uniqueness and should move toward empirically grounded, probabilistic approaches modelled on DNA typing.
athar_applications: Frames the historical story ATHAR can tell: from 'individualisation' claims to probabilistic evidence.
limitations: Perspective piece; uses wrongful-conviction data from before 2005.

title: Interpretation of statistical evidence in criminal trials: The prosecutor's fallacy and the defense attorney's fallacy
key_findings: Named and described two reasoning errors with statistical evidence: treating P(evidence|innocent) as P(innocent|evidence) (prosecutor's fallacy) and dismissing evidence because many people share a trait (defence attorney's fallacy).
athar_applications: Core forensic-statistics lesson for 16+: a 'transposed conditional' detector mini-game with fictional numbers.
limitations: Older experimental work with mock jurors; terminology now standard.

title: A hierarchy of propositions: deciding which level to address in casework
key_findings: Introduced the hierarchy of propositions (source, activity, offence levels) for framing what a forensic scientist's evaluation addresses.
athar_applications: Teaches 'whose is it?' vs 'how did it get there?' vs 'did a crime happen?' - three different questions.
limitations: Foundational but older; later refined by ENFSI 2015 and ISFG 2018.

title: DNA commission of the International Society for Forensic Genetics: Assessing the value of forensic biological evidence - Guidelines highlighting the importance of propositions
key_findings: International commission guidance on formulating propositions for biological evidence, stressing the gap between sub-source/source conclusions and activity-level questions.
athar_applications: Underpins ATHAR rule: a DNA 'hit' in a case must be paired with a transfer/activity question.
limitations: Expert-commission recommendations; practice adoption varies.

title: DNA transfer in forensic science: A review
key_findings: Reviews research on how DNA is transferred directly and indirectly, how it persists and how background DNA complicates interpretation.
athar_applications: Basis for the 'DNA transfer' virtual lab (abstract tokens moving between fictional objects/people).
limitations: Review; quantitative transfer rates vary widely by conditions; findings summarised from scope - expert to confirm.

title: The 'CSI Effect': Does It Really Exist?
publisher: National Institute of Justice (NIJ Journal, Issue 259)
key_findings: Survey of 1,027 summoned jurors (Michigan, 2006): 46% expected some scientific evidence in every criminal case; CSI viewers had higher expectations.
Higher expectations did not translate into a general demand for scientific evidence before convicting; only 4 of 13 scenarios showed viewer/non-viewer differences, inconsistent in direction.
Authors propose a broader 'tech effect' rather than a show-specific CSI effect.
athar_applications: Report the CSI effect honestly as weakly supported; ATHAR's 'myth' modules should not overclaim TV harm.
limitations: Single county sample; self-reported hypothetical verdicts; magazine summary of a study, not the full peer-reviewed paper.

title: Crime-Show-Viewing Habits and Public Attitudes Toward Forensic Evidence: The 'CSI Effect' Revisited
key_findings: Survey study of whether crime-show viewing relates to public attitudes about forensic evidence (part of the mixed CSI-effect literature).
athar_applications: Adds to the evidence base that CSI-effect claims are mixed; supports cautious wording.
limitations: Findings not captured in-session (no abstract in Crossref record) - expert to summarise before use.

title: Investigating CSI: Portrayals of DNA testing on a forensic crime show and their potential effects
key_findings: Content analysis of how DNA testing is portrayed on CSI and discussion of possible effects on public understanding.
athar_applications: Source list of concrete TV distortions of DNA (speed, certainty) for the CSI-myths file.
limitations: Findings summarised from scope; content analysis does not measure audience effects directly.

title: Virtual reality for teaching and learning in crime scene investigation
key_findings: Reports on using VR for teaching crime scene investigation in higher education (study details not captured in-session).
athar_applications: Evidence that virtual scenes are an accepted teaching tool; informs ATHAR's 2D/3D scene documentation lab.
limitations: University context, not teens; outcome measures not captured - expert to summarise.

title: Misapplication of Forensic Science (Innocence Project issue page)
key_findings: States misapplied forensic science contributed to more than half of Innocence Project wrongful-conviction cases and nearly a quarter of all wrongful convictions since 1989 (the earlier, now-removed page gave 52% and 24%, the latter attributed to the National Registry of Exonerations).

Lists bite mark analysis, hair comparison, toolmarks, arson investigation, fingerprint analysis, dog scent evidence, comparative bullet lead analysis, shaken baby syndrome diagnosis and bloodstain pattern analysis as methods whose foundations were shown to be weak.
athar_applications: Advocacy context for ATHAR's 'why limits matter' framing; numbers must be cited with their scope (IP caseload vs all US exonerations).
limitations: Advocacy organisation; page undated; percentages depend on case selection and definitions - prefer ATH-SRC-0336 for analysis.
AUDIT 2026-10-27: original URL (overturning-wrongful-convictions-involving-flawed-forensics) returns 404; replaced by the live issue page, which supports the same figures in rounded form.

title: The National Registry of Exonerations
authors: Michigan State University College of Law
Newkirk Center for Science & Society (UC Irvine)
key_findings: Homepage at fetch reported 3,868 exonerations and more than 36,226 years lost since 1989; 'false or misleading forensic evidence' is one coded contributing factor.
athar_applications: Data source for adult-reviewer background only; ATHAR must not reproduce real victims' or exonerees' cases for teens without editorial review.
limitations: US only; counts change continuously; contributing-factor breakdown not visible on fetched homepage.

title: Crime Scene Investigation: A Guide for Law Enforcement (NCJ 243598)
authors: Technical Working Group on Crime Scene Investigation (2000)
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Organises scene work into stages: arrival and priorities; preliminary documentation and evaluation; processing; completing and recording; equipment - each with principle, policy, procedure.
athar_applications: Principle-level structure for ATHAR's scene-documentation lab (secure, observe, record, then collect) - procedures kept generic.
limitations: Operational law-enforcement manual; ATHAR must use only high-level principles and never reproduce procedural detail.

title: SWGDRUG Recommendations (Scientific Working Group for the Analysis of Seized Drugs)
authors: Scientific Working Group for the Analysis of Seized Drugs (SWGDRUG)
key_findings: Current edition 8.2 approved 27 June 2024; internationally used minimum standards and best practice for seized-drug examination; earlier versions archived.
athar_applications: Teaches the principle that identification relies on combining independent analytical techniques of different discriminating power (abstract only - no chemistry procedures in ATHAR).
limitations: Category A/B/C technique scheme not read in-session; operational chemistry content is out of scope for teen content.

title: SWGDE - Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (published documents)
authors: Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence
key_findings: Consensus documents on digital and multimedia evidence organised by committees: Audio, Cellular & Geolocation, Forensics, Imaging, Photography, Quality & Standards, Video; drafts released for public comment.
12 SWGDE documents are on the OSAC Registry (see ATH-SRC-0309).
athar_applications: Reference for forensic imaging and digital-evidence cards (image authentication, photo documentation principles).
limitations: Site footer: copyright SWGDE, documents need written permission for unauthorised use; individual documents not read in-session.

title: CFReDS - Computer Forensic Reference Data Sets
authors: NIST Information Technology Laboratory (Software Security Group)
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: Repository of simulated digital evidence with documented contents (e.g., seeded search strings) for tool validation, training and proficiency testing; partly NIJ-funded.
athar_applications: Model for ATHAR: build fictional digital-evidence 'disk images' with documented ground truth for scoring learner reasoning.
limitations: Datasets aimed at professionals; specific terms of use not read; some datasets contributed by third parties may carry other terms.

title: Bringing science to digital forensics with standardized forensic corpora
key_findings: Argues for standardised forensic corpora (realistic but non-sensitive data sets) to make digital forensics research and education reproducible.
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's approach of fully fictional, documented data sets for digital-evidence cases.
limitations: 2009 technology context; DFRWS proceedings special issue.
AUDIT 2026-10-27: Crossref lists a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 version-of-record licence (from 2019) and OpenAlex marks it hybrid OA; rights corrected from COPYRIGHTED_RESTRICTED/paywalled.

title: Scientific Working Group for Forensic Toxicology (SWGTOX) Standard Practices for Method Validation in Forensic Toxicology
authors: Scientific Working Group for Forensic Toxicology (SWGTOX)
publisher: Oxford University Press (Journal of Analytical Toxicology)
key_findings: Sets minimum validation parameters a forensic toxicology method must demonstrate before casework use (e.g., bias, precision, limits, interferences, carryover).
athar_applications: Principle for the toxicology card: results are only as good as the validated method; no substances or doses are discussed in ATHAR.
limitations: Believed superseded by ANSI/ASB Standard 036 (not verified in-session); validation parameter list summarised from known scope - expert check needed.

title: Estimation of the time since death in the early post-mortem period
key_findings: Review of methods for estimating time since death in the early period, emphasising that estimates are ranges with stated uncertainty and that combining methods narrows but never eliminates uncertainty.
athar_applications: Corrects TV myth of exact time of death; ATHAR shows only interval estimates with widening uncertainty (no body imagery).
limitations: Technical medical review; ATHAR uses only the principle of interval estimation; details summarised from known scope - expert check needed.

title: Evidentiary Standards for Forensic Anthropology
key_findings: Discusses how forensic anthropology methods should meet evidentiary standards (testability, known error rates, standards) and the need for validated, population-appropriate methods.
athar_applications: Supports the anthropology card: biological-profile estimates (age, sex, stature) are probabilistic ranges and population-dependent.
limitations: US legal frame (Daubert); details summarised from title/scope - expert check needed.

title: The end of the (forensic science) world as we know it? The example of trace evidence
key_findings: Argues trace evidence has declined in casework despite its value, partly due to DNA dominance and managerial pressures, and calls for a broader, intelligence-led view of forensic science.
athar_applications: Supports ATHAR's choice to feature fibres/glass/soil as reasoning-rich, visually safe clue types.
limitations: Position paper from a specific school (Lausanne/Sydney); part of a Royal Society theme issue on forensic science.

title: Age estimation in adults by dental imaging assessment systematic review
key_findings: Systematic review of dental-imaging methods for estimating adult age (findings not captured in-session).
athar_applications: Illustrates that age estimation produces ranges with method-dependent error - contrast with discredited bitemark comparison.
limitations: Abstract not captured; summary limited to scope - expert to confirm conclusions.

title: Latent Fingerprint Examination: A Quality and Gap Analysis (AAAS Forensic Science Assessments)
authors: American Association for the Advancement of Science (Latent Fingerprint Examination Working Group, chair William C. Thompson)
publisher: American Association for the Advancement of Science
key_findings: Assesses what is and is not scientifically established about latent print examination, building on NRC 2009, with 14 recommendations as a research roadmap; second of a two-part series after fire investigation.
athar_applications: Independent (non-government) assessment to pair with PCAST for balanced fingerprint content.
limitations: Publication year not shown on fetched page (believed 2017, unconfirmed); specific findings not read.

title: Academy Standards Board (ASB) of the American Academy of Forensic Sciences
authors: American Academy of Forensic Sciences - Academy Standards Board
key_findings: ASB develops consensus forensic standards within an ANSI-accredited framework; examples shown include ANSI/ASB 113 (identification criteria in forensic toxicology), 098 (mass spectral analysis in toxicology), 011 (scope of expertise in forensic document examination), 096 (examination and documentation of ammunition).
athar_applications: Points ATHAR reviewers to discipline-specific standards (toxicology identification criteria; document-examiner scope).
limitations: Individual standards' editions/status not read in-session; ASB is one of several SDOs (ASTM, ISO).

title: Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences (CSFS)
key_findings: UK-based professional body offering membership grades and a Chartered Forensic Practitioner designation, publishing Science & Justice, and setting standards for educational courses and CPD; reported FSR Code v2 effective 2 Oct 2025.
athar_applications: Potential partner/reviewer body for scientific review of ATHAR content (course-accreditation experience).
limitations: Organisation page; royal charter status not confirmed on fetched page.

title: Forensic Analysis: Weighing Bullet Lead Evidence
authors: Committee on Scientific Assessment of Bullet Lead Elemental Composition Comparison
key_findings: FBI-requested assessment: the elemental measurement technique (ICP-OES, seven elements) was judged analytically sound.

But interpretation was overstated: bullets are not unique like DNA; analysis cannot link a bullet to a particular box or date; experts should not state the probability a bullet came from the defendant because distribution data are lacking.
Criticised FBI statistical grouping methods ('chaining', undocumented 2-SD overlap) and called for proper statistics, acknowledgement of coincidental matches, and better QA/proficiency testing.
athar_applications: Teaches a subtle, high-value lesson: a measurement can be accurate while the inference drawn from it is invalid (precise chemistry, weak conclusion).
limitations: Weapon-adjacent topic: use only as an abstract 18+ case study; the FBI later stopped the practice (per secondary sources, not verified in-session).

title: A Review of the FBI's Handling of the Brandon Mayfield Case (Unclassified and Redacted)
authors: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General (Oversight and Review Division)
publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General
rights_jurisdiction: US (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105); status outside US not established
key_findings: An unusual similarity between the latent print (LFP 17) and Mayfield's known print, surfaced by the IAFIS database search, misled three FBI examiners and a court-appointed expert; the true source (Daoud) was not in IAFIS.
A significant cause was reasoning backward from Mayfield's known prints ('circular reasoning'): ambiguous features in the latent were read as matching points.

Other causes: reliance on tiny Level 3 details that did not correspond to the true donor; inadequate explanations for differences under the 'one discrepancy rule'; failure to re-examine after the Spanish authorities' negative report.
OIG found no compelling evidence that the non-blind verification procedure caused this error, but recommended blind-verification alternatives and documenting latent features before comparison.
OIG found no evidence that high-profile pressure was a significant cause.
athar_applications: Anchor real-world case (adult-reviewer reference) for 'document the evidence before seeing the suspect' (linear sequential unmasking) and for AFIS 'close non-match' risk in large databases.
Teaching point: experienced, multiple, concurring examiners can all be wrong when the procedure lets the reference shape the reading of the trace.
limitations: Single-case investigation; redacted. Its causal attributions are the OIG's judgments, not experimental findings.
Involves terrorism and religion; sensitive for teen content. Use as background for designers, not as a playable case.
